panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of the hill-fort silhouetted at dusk
panels.action: Vīr Narayan stands armored on the stone ramparts of Chauragarh, jaw set, as dark forests and steep ridges fall away below and distant Mughal banners gather like a storm on the horizon.

dialogue.text: In 1564, as Akbar’s armies closed on Chauragarh, a young prince named Vīr Narayan chose a hill of stone for his last stand—and a kingdom’s treasure and women chose fire.

i18n.hi: १५६४ में, जब अकबर की फ़ौजें चौरागढ़ पर चढ़ आईं, जवान राजकुमार वीर नारायण ने अपनी आखिरी जंग के लिए पत्थर की चोटी चुनी—और राज्य का ख़ज़ाना व स्त्रियाँ आग को।

panels.shot: high aerial wide of the Satpura range with labels absent, focusing on terrain
panels.action: The Satpura hills roll in dense green waves; a single rocky height, crowned with battlements and towers, rises above forests and ravines, with a narrow path snaking up to a fortified gate.

dialogue.text: South of the Narmada, in the Satpura hills, stood Chauragarh—a Gond hill-fort piled on a crag, a storehouse of elephants, coin and grain, and the last refuge of Garha-Katanga’s royal house.

i18n.hi: नर्मदा के दक्षिण, सतपुड़ा की पहाड़ियों में चौरागढ़ खड़ा था—चट्टान पर टिका गोंड किला, हाथियों, सिक्कों और अनाज का भंडार, गढ़ा-कटंगा की रानी की आखिरी शरण।

panels.shot: medium close-up on Vīr Narayan in shadowed corridor, light from one side
panels.action: Inside a stone hall lit by oil lamps, Vīr Narayan, young yet stern, grips the hilt of his sword, listening to distant drumbeats as courtiers and warriors, tense and weary, watch him for direction.

dialogue.text: Abu’l Fazl’s Akbarnama tells us that after Rani Durgavati fell at Narrai, her son Vīr Narayan withdrew here, gathering the remnants of the army, sealing the gates, and waiting for Asaf Khan’s return.

i18n.hi: अबुल फ़ज़्ल की आकबरनामा बताती है कि नरrai पर रानी दुर्गावती के गिरने के बाद, उनका बेटा वीर नारायण यहाँ आया, बचे-सखे सिपाही समेटे, फाटक बंद किए, और आसफ़ ख़ाँ की वापसी की राह देखी।

panels.shot: slow push-in from behind Vīr Narayan looking out over the landscape
panels.action: From the battlements, Vīr Narayan looks out over forested valleys where long dust-plumes and glittering lines of troops wind towards the hill, Mughal standards and war-elephants visible among them.

dialogue.text: The Mughals had already tasted Garha’s wealth at Narrai. Now, as Nizamuddin Ahmad notes, they marched on the fort that guarded its hoards and nearly a thousand war-elephants.

i18n.hi: मुग़ल नरrai पर ही गढ़ा की दौलत चख चुके थे। अब, जैसा निज़ामुद्दीन अहमद लिखता है, वे उस किले पर बढ़े जो उसके ख़ज़ाने और करीब हज़ार जंगी हाथियों की रखवाली करता था।

panels.shot: crowded courtyard wide, slightly elevated angle
panels.action: In the inner courtyard, Gond warriors tighten armor and string bows; women of the court in heavy ornaments stand with children and elders, faces drawn, while Vīr Narayan addresses his captains.

dialogue.speaker: vir_narayan_and_the_defenders_of_chauragarh
dialogue.text: We hold the hill. As long as these stones stand, Garha is not yet taken.

i18n.hi: हम यह पहाड़ी थामे हैं। जब तक ये पत्थर हैं, गढ़ा नहीं टूटा।

panels.shot: dynamic low-angle of Mughal vanguard approaching
panels.action: Lines of Mughal matchlock-men, archers, and armoured horsemen move through the forest foot of the hill; towering elephants with howdahs carry officers, their silhouettes sharp against the sky.

dialogue.text: Asaf Khan, Akbar’s commander, had already broken the Gond field army. Now, with imperial sanction and the scent of plunder, his men ringed Chauragarh and began their slow, grinding advance.

i18n.hi: अकबर का सेनापति आसफ़ ख़ाँ गोंडों की मैदानी फ़ौज पहले ही तोड़ चुका था। अब बादशाही इजाज़त और लूट की बू के साथ, उसके सिपाही चौरागढ़ को घेरकर धीमी, घिसटती चढ़ाई पर लग गए।

panels.shot: defensive wall-level wide of first assault
panels.action: Gond defenders at the parapet hurl stones and flaming bundles down a steep, narrow approach; below, Mughal troops raise shields and ladders, some stumbling on the rough slope under the bombardment.

dialogue.text: Abu’l Fazl records that they met fierce resistance. For days, perhaps weeks, every ascent was punished—stones and fire greeted each ladder, and the hill itself fought for its people.

i18n.hi: अबुल फ़ज़्ल लिखता है कि उन्हें ज़बरदस्त टक्कर मिली। कई दिन, शायद हफ्तों तक, हर चढ़ाई की सज़ा मिली—हर सीढ़ी पर पत्थर और आग बरसे, मानो खुद पहाड़ अपने लोगों के लिए लड़ पड़ा हो।

panels.shot: medium action shot of Vīr Narayan in combat on rampart
panels.action: On a cramped stretch of wall, Vīr Narayan, armor scuffed, swings his sword to knock away a Mughal soldier’s spear, pushing back attackers as smoke curls and arrows thud into the stone around him.

dialogue.text: The Akbarnama does not romanticise him, yet it notes simply that Vīr Narayan fought bravely. In those few words, a young prince becomes a commander, trading the safety of heirs for the duty of a wall-top fighter.

i18n.hi: आकबरनामा उसे नायक नहीं बनाता, बस इतना कहता है कि वीर नारायण डटकर लड़ा। वही कुछ शब्दों में जवान राजकुमार से सेनानायक बन जाता है—वारिस की सुरक्षा छोड़, दीवार पर लड़ाकू बन खड़ा होता है।

panels.shot: interior hall, dim, intimate medium shot
panels.action: In a dim chamber within the fort, court women sit in a tight circle, oil lamps casting long shadows; one elder woman, dignified and resolute, clasps a younger woman’s hands as they listen to distant battle sounds.

dialogue.text: Gond and later traditions speak of Kamala Devi leading the women of the court. The chronicles simply tell us that, as the fight worsened, the women within chose a different weapon than steel.

i18n.hi: गोंड और बाद की परंपराएँ कहती हैं कि कमला देवी ने दरबार की स्त्रियों का नेतृत्व किया। इतिहासनामे बस इतना बताते हैं कि लड़ाई बिगड़ने पर भीतर की स्त्रियों ने इस्पात से अलग हथियार चुना।

panels.shot: somber interior wide focusing on preparations around a central pit
panels.action: Within a courtyard, women pour oil and stack wood into a deep pit; some embrace each other in silence, some cradle children, their faces set, firelight from torches beginning to flicker on their ornaments.

dialogue.text: Both Abu’l Fazl and Nizamuddin record that before the gates fell, the royal women and many others performed jauhar—mass self-immolation—choosing flames over capture and the unknown that lay beyond conquest.

i18n.hi: अबुल फ़ज़्ल और निज़ामुद्दीन दोनों लिखते हैं कि फाटक टूटने से पहले, रानियों और कई औरतों ने जौहर किया—सामूहिक अग्नि-समर्पण—कैद और फ़तह के बाद के अँधेरे से पहले ही आग को चुम लिया।

panels.shot: tight focus on Vīr Narayan’s profile in flickering firelight
panels.action: Vīr Narayan stands in a corridor, face half-lit by a distant glow, eyes closed for a moment as the reflection of rising flame dances on his steel helmet; behind him, a young warrior waits for orders.

dialogue.text: The sources do not tell us what words, if any, passed between prince and women before the fire. They only preserve the order of events: the blaze within, then the final push at the gate without.

i18n.hi: मूलों में नहीं लिखा कि आग से पहले राजकुमार और स्त्रियों के बीच क्या बात हुई, अगर हुई तो। बस क्रम बचा है—पहले भीतर की ज्वाला, फिर बाहर फाटक पर आखिरी धक्का।

panels.action: At the main gate, its wooden beams broken, Gond defenders clash with advancing Mughal troops in a swirl of dust; Vīr Narayan, in the thick of the fight, raises his sword to rally the last line.

dialogue.text: When the assault finally broke through, the battle narrowed to corridors and courtyards. Abu’l Fazl states that Vīr Narayan was killed in this struggle, falling as the fort was being taken.

i18n.hi: जब हमला आखिरकार टूटकर भीतर घुसा, जंग गलियारों और आँगनों में सिमट गई। अबुल फ़ज़्ल लिखता है कि इसी धक्का-मुक्की में वीर नारायण मारे गए, जब किला हाथ से निकल रहा था।

panels.shot: somber interior wide of blackened courtyard after fire
panels.action: The same courtyard where the pyre was prepared now lies blackened and empty, smoke still curling from charred beams; a few discarded bangles lie half-buried in ash, while armed men pass by in the background.

dialogue.text: The chronicles pass over details; they move quickly from this courtyard of ash to ledgers of spoils. Yet the fire at Chauragarh remains a stark entry—recorded, not embellished, and left to speak by itself.

i18n.hi: इतिहासनामे बारीकी छोड़ देते हैं; वे इस राख भरे आँगन से सीधे लूट के हिसाब-किताब पर कूद जाते हैं। फिर भी चौरागढ़ की आग अलग दर्ज है—लिखी गई, न सजाई, और खुद बोलने को छोड़ दी गई।

panels.action: Inside a large storeroom, Mughal officers supervise as chests of coins, jewels, and gold ornaments are pried open; scribes seated on the floor note down figures while guards stand watch amid stacked wealth.

dialogue.text: Abu’l Fazl lists the plunder in careful detail—chests of coin, ornaments and valuables from the Gond treasury—describing how Asaf Khan seized the accumulated wealth of Garha-Katanga along with its stronghold.

i18n.hi: अबुल फ़ज़्ल लूट का हिसाब तफसील से देता है—सिक्कों के संदूक, गोंड ख़ज़ाने के ज़ेवर और कीमती सामान—बताता है कैसे आसफ़ ख़ाँ ने गढ़ा-कटंगा की जमा-दौलत उसके किले समेत झटक ली।

panels.shot: expansive outdoor wide of elephant enclosures
panels.action: Long lines of war-elephants stand tethered in rough stockades near the fort, mahouts on their necks; in the distance, more elephants are led down forest paths, forming a vast and ordered herd.

dialogue.text: The Akbarnama claims close to a thousand elephants were taken. The Ain-i-Akbari later notes Garha’s elephant-rich lands in imperial registers, showing how this living wealth was a key prize of the campaign.

i18n.hi: आकबरनामा कहता है कि करीब हज़ार हाथी पकड़े गए। बाद में आई आईन-ए-अकबरी में गढ़ा की हाथी-समृद्ध ज़मीनें रजिस्टर में दर्ज हैं, दिखाती हैं कि ये ज़िंदा दौलत इस मुहिम की बड़ी फ़तेह थी।

panels.shot: medium shot of Mughal officers in heated discussion near elephants
panels.action: Near a cluster of elephants, Asaf Khan, richly dressed, gestures toward the herd while subordinate officers whisper; a few elephants are marked with bright cloths, suggesting some are being set apart.

dialogue.text: Yet Abu’l Fazl also records another detail: of nearly a thousand elephants, Asaf Khan reportedly sent only about two hundred to Akbar, keeping most for himself, a choice that would briefly cost him imperial favour.

i18n.hi: फिर भी अबुल फ़ज़्ल एक और बात दर्ज करता है: करीब हज़ार हाथियों में से आसफ़ ख़ाँ ने कहते हैं कि सिर्फ़ दो सौ के आसपास अकबर को भेजे, बाक़ी अपने पास रखे—और इसी लालच ने कुछ समय को उसकी बादशाही नज़र में गिरावट ला दी।

panels.shot: courtly interior wide of Akbar’s darbar, with distant figure of Asaf Khan
panels.action: In a richly decorated Mughal hall, Akbar sits on a low, wide throne surrounded by courtiers; at a distance, a figure representing Asaf Khan stands bowed, while a courtier reads from a scroll before the emperor.

dialogue.text: Nizamuddin Ahmad’s Tabaqat-i-Akbari notes that Asaf Khan’s handling of the spoils drew scrutiny. Called to account, he was compelled to bring in what he had held back, a reminder that greed could shake even a victor’s standing.

i18n.hi: निज़ामुद्दीन अहमद की तबकात-ए-अकबरी लिखती है कि आसफ़ ख़ाँ की लूट-बाँट पर शक उठा। हिसाब के लिए बुलाया गया, तो उसे छिपाई हुई दौलत भी लौटानी पड़ी—सबक कि लालच, फ़तह पाने वाले की कुर्सी भी डिगा सकता है।

panels.shot: map-like overhead of Garha-Katanga with Mughal banners appearing
panels.action: A stylised view of central India shows the lands of Garha-Katanga shaded, the Narmada and Satpura marked by rivers and hills; Mughal banners and tiny elephants spread across the region, overlaying Gond settlements.

dialogue.text: After Chauragarh, Garha-Katanga did not vanish. The Ain-i-Akbari records it piece by piece—districts, revenues, elephants—folded into the Mughal empire, its hill-kingdom recast as a line in an imperial register.

i18n.hi: चौरागढ़ के बाद गढ़ा-कटंगा ग़ायब नहीं हुआ। आईन-ए-अकबरी उसे टुकड़ों में दर्ज करती है—परगने, महसूल, हाथी—सब मुग़ल सल्तनत में जोड़े गए, पहाड़ी रियासत बादशाही रजिस्टर की एक पंक्ति बनकर रह गई।

panels.shot: evening wide of ruined yet standing fort with ghostly overlay of past defenders
panels.action: At dusk, the silhouette of Chauragarh’s walls rises quiet against the sky; in the fading light, faint, almost transparent figures of Vīr Narayan and Gond defenders seem to stand once more along the ramparts.

dialogue.text: From Abu’l Fazl and Nizamuddin’s pages, we see Chauragarh as both fortress and ledger—where a prince died, women entered fire, and a thousand elephants changed masters—and we are left to decide what, in that smoke, endures as loss and what as memory.

i18n.hi: अबुल फ़ज़्ल और निज़ामुद्दीन के सफ़ों से चौरागढ़ हमें किले और खाताबही दोनों की तरह दिखता है—जहाँ एक राजकुमार मरा, स्त्रियाँ आग में उतरीं, और हज़ार हाथी मालिक बदले—और हम पर छोड़ा गया कि उस धुएँ में क्या सिर्फ़ नुक़सान है, और क्या बनी हुई याद।

title_i18n.en: Chauragarh Falls and the Fire Behind the Gates
title_i18n.hi: चौरागढ़ जलप्रपात और फाटकों के पीछे की आग
